# From philosophy to practice --- defining your research question and design {#sec-question-and-design}

Eimear Dolan

*School of Arts, Sciences and Humanities and Centre of Lifestyle Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo, SP, BR.*

## Introduction {#introduction-1}

In [Chapter 1](01-foundations.qmd), several topics were discussed: What is truth? What is knowledge? How can we go about discovering truth or knowledge? What values do you hold as a scientist? What is logic and how can we use it to infer meaning from empirical data? These are important philosophical questions, and I agree with James, in that reflecting on them has had a large and positive impact on how I approach and conduct my own research. They are also highly complex and individual. You may, and probably should, find yourself returning to Chapter 1 several times, and you may take something different from it every time, depending on where you are in your research journey at any given time.

At some point, however, we need to move from philosophy to practice. One thing that you will read again and again throughout this book is that "*it depends on your research question*". The practicalities of designing and implementing a research study involve hundreds, if not thousands of small decisions and the research process is full of forking paths. A well-formulated and clearly defined research question acts as both your foundation, and your north star, guiding you throughout this process. Every time you are faced with a decision, you must ask yourself "*what does this mean for my research question?"*. If you are ensure about what your research question actually is, chances are, you will spend a large part of your research journey feeling somewhat lost and anchorless. As such, if you cannot clearly state the question your study is designed to answer, you need to stop and reflect on this, before proceeding further.

As with most things involving research and science, there are no straightforward answers or automated responses here. The purpose of this chapter, therefore, is to delve into this topic, by reflecting on what exactly a research question is, and providing some guidance on how you may approach defining yours. Your research question should ultimately shape the decisions you make about every other aspect of your research design, and this chapter is intended to act as a bridge to connect you from the philosophical concepts described in Chapter 1, to the more practical advice on participant recruitment ([Chapter 3](03-participants.qmd)), quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis ([Chapters 4](04-quantitative-data-collection.qmd)–[7](07-qualitative-analysis.qmd)), secondary research approaches ([Chapter 8](08-secondary-research.qmd)) and writing up research articles and submitting for peer review ([Chapter 9](09-writing-and-peer-review.qmd)), described throughout the rest of this book.

Throughout this chapter, I will operationally define key terms that will come up at several points throughout this book. It is possible that these may differ to what you have seen elsewhere, even within this book, and there are no universally accepted definitions for many of these. What is important, however, is not that we all use identical terms, or even whether we completely agree with others definitions, but instead that we clearly define and explain the terms that we are using, so that we can understand and discuss our points of agreement and disagreement. On this point, I echo James' recommendation from [Chapter 1](01-foundations.qmd) -- don't get too caught up in terminology or labels. Instead, reflect on the underlying concepts and what they may mean for your own research question and project, and make decisions that will allow you to answer this question as completely as possible, and to articulate your thought process as best you can throughout your research journey.

## So what actually is a research question? {#ch02-so-what-actually-is-a-research-question}

During my initial conversations with potential research students, we generally start by discussing the broad topic area that they are interested in investigating, *e.g.,* the influence of energy availability on health and performance, or whether hormonal fluctuations throughout the menstrual cycle may influence exercise performance or response to training. Within these broad topics, there are multiple questions that could potentially be answered, and so at some stage we need to progress from the broader topic area, to the specific research problem that we want to tackle in this particular study. From this, the research question, along with the study aims and objectives naturally follows. In other words, we need to identify what specific issue, uncertainty or research gap within the broader topic area we will focus our attention on. For example, in a recent study related to energy availability and bone health, we recognized that although there is currently a substantial body of evidence to suggest that energy availability may influence bone health, little is known about whether the macronutrient composition of available energy impacts these responses. This was the research problem within the broader topic that we wanted to focus our attention on. From this, we then needed to start thinking about the specific research question that we would address within our study. This question should identify the exact aspect of the broader problem that the study specifically seeks to address and allows for conversion of the broader problem into something that can be empirically tested. In this example, the question we settled on, after considering various possibilities, was "*What are the effects of short-term low energy availability, with varying protein contents, on the acute bone biomarker response to exercise?".* We then thought about how to present this in terms of the overarching research aim, which is a concise statement of the overall purpose of the study. In this example we described this aim as "*to examine the effects of short-term low energy availability, with and without preserved protein intake, on the acute bone biomarker responses to exercise in healthy adults*" [@dolanBoneBiomarkerInflammatory2026]. Finally, this overarching aim should be translated into specific, clearly defined objectives that clarify exactly how this aim can be reached. This can include operational definitions of all relevant terms within the stated aim, *e.g.,* by defining what we mean by "short-term low energy availability", how protein preservation can be achieved and which exact bone biomarkers will be measured.

This example of progression from broad topic area to focused research aims and objectives is summarized in [Table 1](#table-ch02-1), and I encourage you to fill in the second row of the table with your own research topic, problem, question, aims and objectives. As you can see, these concepts are closely related, but each serve a subtly different purpose, with the research problem providing the rationale, the question providing the focus, the aim clarifying the overall purpose of the study, while the objectives provide specificity. It is important to highlight, however, that although these aspects tend to progress from each other, with each step gradually narrowing the scope and increasing specificity, you may not necessarily be able to approach this in a strictly linear manner. Developing a research question tends to be an iterative process, and it is likely that you will go forward and backward between these stages several times, further refining and developing your ideas as things progress.

### Types of Research Questions and Designs {#ch02-types-of-research-questions-and-designs}

The research question, and the subsequent aim that arises from this, is not just a statement to include at the end of an introduction paragraph. It is the decision make tool that guides your entire research process, and all aspects of your design and analysis approach should flow directly from this. As described in [Chapter 1](01-foundations.qmd), research questions can be broadly categorized into three broad types, namely descriptive (*e.g.,* what is the frequency of trait X in population Y), predictive (*e.g.,* does parameter X predict occurrence Y) or explanatory (does a change in parameter X lead to a change in outcome Y?). To answer these questions, we must design a study that allows us to collect data capable of answering it, or at least to get us closer to an answer than we were before the study. I consider this latter point important, as in my opinion, few research questions have definitive absolute answers, and the purpose of any single study is rarely to provide absolute answers, but instead to nudge us just a little closer to "truth". For those of you who have read [Chapter 1](01-foundations.qmd), you may recognize that I have demonstrated my perspective as a "critical realist" - individuals with other ontological and epistemological perspectives may have other opinions.

Once you have settled on your research question, you can think about what the most appropriate design to address it may be. Study designs can be broadly categorized as being either observational or experimental. Briefly, observational designs include studies where you observe and collect data based on what is happening in the world, without any intentional manipulation. For example, observational designs may include studies where you collect data on the characteristics of a particular athletic or clinical group, or where you collect data to evaluate common behaviors or characteristics (*e.g.,* physical activity levels or capacities) to identify if they associate with or predict certain outcomes (*e.g.,* disease or injury risk, or probability of competitive success). These observations can be made at a single point in time (cross-sectional), or you could follow your participants and conduct repeated measurements across a period of time (longitudinal). We can also further classify observational studies in relation to the direction of data collection relative to the research question, namely prospective studies where researchers define the study and then collect data moving forward, or retrospective studies, where researchers use existing data such as medical records or existing datasets.

The defining feature of an observational study is the lack of intentional manipulation by the researcher -- the intention is to observe events as they occur. In contrast, an experimental study aims to manipulate some aspect of the environment, to find out whether this manipulation influences another aspect. For example, implementation of a resistance training program to investigate its influence on muscle strength, or providing a sport supplement to investigate its influence on exercise performance, are common types of experimental studies conducted within the broader field of sport and exercise science. Experimental trials can be further considered in relation to important characteristics. For example, inclusion of a control group is generally important to ensure that any effects observed can be attributed to the intervention administered. Ideally individuals should be randomized to all available experimental conditions or orders, *e.g.,* intervention versus control, to reduce the risk of systematic bias within results. It is also useful to think about whether your question would be best addressed by recruiting separate groups to take part in each condition (parallel-group design), or whether you will have the same participant take part in each condition (cross-over group design), and whether it will involve a short, one-off intervention (acute), or a longer duration intervention (chronic).

Some examples of research questions and designs commonly employed in sport and exercise science are summarised in [Table 2](#table-ch02-2). It is important to stress, however, that the broad categories that I use here are intended only to give you examples of the possibilities that are available to you. Categories such as observational or experimental, or quantitative or qualitative, are useful start points, but there are no strict boundaries between these categories, and in my opinion, discussions that pitch different categories against each other, *e.g.,* to describe observational [versus]{.underline} experimental studies, or quantitative [versus]{.underline} qualitative approaches, are rarely useful. Instead, I suggest that you consider the key attributes of each of these broad categories and instead of thinking "*which is best?*", think "*which is the best approach to employ to answer my research question?".* The best design is the one that can best address your research question, and some of the best research sits in those blurry lines between the different categories. You may even find that a mixed approach is valuable as introduced in [Chapter 1](01-foundations.qmd). Keep this in mind throughout this book, and don't get too caught up in "right" versus "wrong" approaches. Instead, keep returning to your question and make decisions that will help you to answer it as best you can.

Categories and design definitions are useful to exemplify the different options available to you, but don't get too caught up in labels and remember that the best design is the one that is best suited to your question.*

#### Frameworks to define and specify your research question & design {#ch02-frameworks-to-define-and-specify-your-research-question-design}

There is a lot to think about in relation to study design and implementation, and subsequent chapters will go into more detail on specific topics. There are various frameworks available that can help you throughout this process. These frameworks cannot provide direct answers as to the most appropriate approach to take to tackle your own research question, but they can provide a guide to help you to organize your thought process. For experimental studies involving the implementation of an intervention, I like to use the PICOS approach to help guide me through the process, which stands for **P**opulation, **I**ntervention, **C**omparator, **O**utcomes and **S**tudy Design. I will now go through each of these to give you an example of how you may apply it to your own study. This is specific to intervention studies, but there are other options that can be used to guide you through other study types, such as PECO (**P**opulation, **E**xposure, **C**omparator, **O**utcome), **C**o**C**o**P**op (Condition, Context, Population) or **SPIDER** (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research Type).

I will briefly go through the PICOS framework now, and I encourage you to use these examples to summarise the key design elements of your study. Don't get too bogged down in detail at this stage. The idea is not to finalise every aspect of your research question and design in a single session -- this is a continuous and iterative process, not a one-off task to check off your to-do list. My usual approach to study design is start out using pen and paper to sketch out my initial thoughts within these broad categories. I don't make final decisions, and I rarely have all the answers, but it does help me to decide what I need to tackle next. And that is basically what research is all about. Figuring out the next problem to solve, solving it, then moving to the next one.

*Population*

In Chapter 3, McCrum et al. (LINK) discuss various topics related to participant identification, selection and recruitment. In order to apply the information described in this chapter to your own study, you first need to think about who you need to recruit to answer your research question. Initially, you can focus on broad characteristics, including your target populations' age, sex, health and training status. Once you have sketched a general outline, you may need to start thinking more deeply about particular aspects. For example, if you plan to work with an athletic group, you will need to define what training level you will target, *e.g.,* using a classification framework (McKay et al.), or to apply some criteria about how you will define important concepts such as "resistance trained".

*Intervention:*

Assuming you are conducting an experimental study, you need to think about the precise details of the intervention that you will use. How long should it be? If it is a nutritional supplement intervention, what dose will you use? If it is a training program, what frequency, timing, type and intensity will you apply? What kind of control and standardization procedures do you need to consider to ensure that any changes that occur can be isolated to the intervention itself? Or, if it is an observational study, these questions apply to the exposure that participants will have experienced either retrospectively or prospectively.

*Comparator:*

Research studies generally involve comparing your results against some form of reference value and it is important to think in advance about what that might be for your particular question. For an intervention study, it is common to include a control group asked to maintain their usual habits during the intervention period, or perhaps who takes a placebo in the case of a nutritional study. In this case, you may compare changes in the control/placebo group versus those in the intervention group, to determine whether any differences pre-post intervention can really be isolated to the intervention itself, and were not due to changes across time that could have happened with or without your intervention.

When thinking of comparators, it is common to think in terms of control or placebo groups, or perhaps two different interventions that vary in some important aspect such as intensity. But the notion of comparing your results against some reference value is relevant in all research studies. For example in a cross-sectional observational study you may wish to compare the data you collect against published normative data, or from a reference population that you collect data from, or take from the literature. Even in qualitative studies, where the focus is on evaluating qualities, as opposed to quantities, there will be some element of comparison, *e.g.,* comparing the answers that your participants provide against what may be expected based on theory, or comparing the responses provided by different participants in terms of their consistency or diversity. Further details on both quantitative and qualitative data analysis approaches are described in [Chapters 6](06-interviewing.qmd) and [7](07-qualitative-analysis.qmd). The first step in developing an analysis plan is, however, to be able to very clearly articulate your research question and precisely what it is you want to know at the end of this.

*Outcomes:*

In [Figure 1](01-foundations.qmd#figure-ch01-1), Chapter 1, James described the conceptual building blocks of research, with the final one being the sources of information available to us, or in other words, the data that we can collect to support us in answering our research question. Generally, you will start out thinking about your research outcomes (or objects of inquiry as described in Chapter 1) as broad constructs, *e.g.,* muscle strength, cardiovascular fitness, or an individual's perception of some event or phenomena. But it is important to keep in mind that these are latent constructs that can never be truly known. Instead, we collect data that provides an indirect estimation of our broader object of inquiry. For example, muscle strength could be estimated by evaluating how much weight an individual can lift for a set number of reps using specific movements and muscle groups. Cardiovascular fitness could be estimated using a graded exercise test to volitional fatigue, with peak aerobic consumption values recorded, or by using a submaximal test and using equations to estimate the individuals' likely maximal values. It could also be assessed by monitoring heart rate at different intensities and during recovery, or by estimating ventilatory thresholds. Information about an individuals perception of some event could be assessed via questionnaire, or interviews or during a focus group. These different options will vary in terms of how closely they represent the "true" construct of interest. For example, evaluating someone's fat free mass via dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) may provide a closer approximation of their muscle mass then assessing via skinfolds and converting using standardized equations. Different assessment protocols will also give different results. For example, the peak power output that someone achieves during an incremental test with 3-minute intervals, can markedly differ to the peak power output achieved during a shorter, more intense protocol. As such, it is important to think very carefully about the different options available to you, and to choose the one that is best aligned with your research question.

Once you have selected your outcomes of interest, it is also important to think about the practicalities of implementing them (see [Chapters 4](04-quantitative-data-collection.qmd) and [6](06-interviewing.qmd) for further detail on quantitative and qualitative data collection). The most important thing in all of this is practice. No one is born knowing how to conduct a research study or to apply technical protocols and it takes time and practice to reach proficiency. Whether it is conducting an interview, an aerobic capacity test or measuring skinfolds, you are likely to mess up the first time you do it. Much better to do that in an informal, training environment under the supervision of a more experienced colleague than with your first research participant. Answering research questions depends on robust and consistent protocol application, so by the time you get to collecting data with actual participants, the protocols should feel like second nature to you.

*Study Design:*

By the time you have thought in detail about all of the above aspects, the overall design will likely be relatively clear, but here is it useful to summarise this, including thinking about the various considerations described above, *e.g.,* whether your study should be randomized, controlled, parallel-group or cross-over. You can also think about other potentially relevant aspects here, for example, if you are offering an intervention and intend to use a cross-over design, how long should you plan between sessions to ensure that residual effects from the first don't impact responses to the next.

**Break Out Box 1:** The Four Question Approach to Outlining a Research Report or Article

::: book-box
Although the specifics will vary according to your specific research question, your department requirements, research group norms or the requirements of the journal that you are submitting to, most research reports and articles will follow a similar broad logic, which can be organized in terms of 4 key questions. These are:

1.  **What is the question?**

*You will address this part in the introduction to your report or article, which you will use to explain, and justify your research question(s), drawing on relevant theory and previous evidence.*

2.  **How did you go about answering this question?**

*You will address this part in the methods section, where you can describe how the study was conducted and how the data were analysed, providing sufficient detail for to ensure that readers can fully understand, evaluate, and even replicate your approach.*

3.  **What was the answer to the question?**

*You will address this in the results section, where you should aim to present the findings results relevant to your research question in as clear, focused and objective a manner as possible.*

4.  **What does this answer mean?**

*You will address this in the discussion section, where you will interpret your results, including their alignment (or lack thereof!) with other research, the strength and limitations of the evidence, potential underpinning mechanisms and implications for future research or practice.*

Further details on writing up a research article and submitting for peer review, including this four question approach to writing a research report or article, are described in more detail in [Chapter 9](09-writing-and-peer-review.qmd). It is useful to keep this in mind throughout the process, however, rather than leaving it to the end of the study when you are focused on writing up. The key point to keep in mind is that each of these sections is dedicated to elaborating a specific aspect of your research question, namely its justification (introduction), the approach used to answer it (methods), the evidence you generate relevant to answering it (results) and what that evidence means (discussion). Without a clear research question, it is very difficult to write a cohesive and aligned research report or article.
:::

### Refining your Research Question {#ch02-refining-your-research-question}

The points raised above are not intended as an exhaustive list of things to consider. Instead, I suggest that you use them as a start-point to get you going. But as I've mentioned at many points, developing a well thought-out and viable research question is not a one-off, stand-alone task. It is a continuous, iterative process, that you need to return to again and again throughout the entire life-span of the project. Below, are some further considerations that I suggest you keep in mind to further refine your research question throughout the process.

#### Scope and feasibility. {#ch02-scope-and-feasibility}

Defining the scope of your research question is difficult, and can become a balancing act between doing something so broad and superficial that the subsequent answer is largely meaningless, to something so narrow and focused that it has little relevance to any real-life situation. All studies will have limitations, which are features of the study that may constrain interpretation, validity or generalizability of the findings, and which are generally things that the research either did not adequately control for, or perhaps could not reasonably avoid. In contrast, a delimit is a boundary deliberately established by the researcher to define the scope of the study. Above, I commented on things you may need to consider in terms of your research population and outcomes of interest. The decisions that you make in terms of these will determine the scope of your study, and in turn, what you can conclude from it. For example, lets say that I deliberately choose to study resistance trained females aged 18-35 years old. This may be a perfectly valid choice for my particular research question, but it means that I cannot inductively generalize my findings to older sedentary males. As such, I have set a boundary on what I can reasonably conclude from my study.

Closely related to the scope of the study is its feasibility. It is very common to begin with highly ambitious plans, but it is important to be realistic about what you can achieve with your current experience level, and within the practical, financial and time constraints of your project. This may be particularly relevant when conducting research as part of a graduate or post-graduate course, where there are often fixed deadlines, limited resources and other competing projects that also require your attention. As such, it is important to differentiate between an interesting research idea and a researchable research question. An idea may be very interesting and potentially valuable, but still be too broad, vague, complex or impractical to investigate within available resources and time-frames. Even for experienced researchers, it is common for different stage of the research project to take considerably longer than anticipated. As such, I highly recommend that you select a question that you can realistically, and that you build in substantial time for reading and training in all study procedures. "*Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good*" is a phrase I find myself using a lot, particularly at the planning stages of a new project. A well-designed and competently executed study is far more valuable than a fantastic idea that never makes it off the page and into practice.

#### How many outcomes should I aim to measure? {#ch02-how-many-outcomes-should-i-aim-to-measure}

Closely related to the issue of scope and feasibility, is the question of how many outcomes should be included. I generally like to think of outcomes in terms of primary, secondary and explanatory outcomes, with each of these terms describing the role that each outcome plays within the study. As you may expect, the primary outcome is the main outcomes used to address the primary research question, and as such, the one(s) that you need to primarily focus on. Your overall design, including any control or standardization procedures applied should focus on this, as will your participant characteristics along with how many of them you need to recruit (see [Chapters 3](03-participants.qmd) and [6](06-interviewing.qmd) for further detail on estimating required sample sizes).

Secondary outcomes are those that are used to address additional research questions related to the intervention or exposure. They provide complementary information, but are not strictly necessary to answer the primary research question. For example, in a study where the primary focus is to evaluate the influence of some sport supplement on 4 km cycling time trial performance, you may also be interested to see whether the same supplement can influence high intensity anaerobic output, and decide to add a Wingate test to your protocol. Closely related, but distinct, is the notion of an explanatory variable. This is an outcome measure that helps you to understand the underlying mechanisms or processes that underpin your primary outcome. As such, although they are not necessary to address your primary question, they may provide important complementary information. For example, in a study whose question is whether 12 weeks of aerobic exercise improves cardiorespiratory fitness in a group of older adults, the primary outcome of interest may be their aerobic capacity, defined as the peak amount of oxygen consumed during an incremental test to volitional fatigue (VO~2Peak~). But you may also be interested in explaining the underlying mechanisms that could explain this change, for example, you may wish to measure outcomes such as stroke volume, ventilatory thresholds, or perhaps mitochondrial or endothelial function. As such, while the primary outcome directly answers the primary research question, the explanatory variables help to explain why that was the case.

Additional outcomes can add both depth (explanatory outcomes) and breadth (secondary outcomes) to your research project and considering how challenging it is to recruit human participants and to conduct a research study, it can be tempting to attempt to add as many outcomes to your design as you can. I do, however, suggest some caution in this approach. Just because you can doesn't necessarily mean that you should, and before adding several additional outcomes, you need to ask yourself A) if your design is appropriately set up to allow for meaningful information to be obtained from them and B) do you have the expertise and other resources (*e.g.,* financial and time) to adequately implement them.

These questions are particularly important when we think in terms of statistical power. For example, in a study where you expect a large effect of your intervention on your primary outcome of interest you may estimate that that you need to recruit approximately 20 people to detect this effect. If the expected effect on secondary or explanatory is far smaller, however, the same sample may be insufficient to adequately investigate them, in which case you must question whether it is really worth the additional time, resources and participant burden in measuring them. Similarly, statistical analyses are often set up with predetermined error rates. The more outcomes you add, the more risk of spurious findings -- a concept termed multiplicity. These, and other, relevant statistical concepts are described in more detail in [Chapter 5](05-quantitative-analysis.qmd), and should be kept in mind when deciding how many outcomes to include in your study.

#### Consider trade-offs associated with different decisions {#ch02-consider-trade-offs-associated-with-different-decisions}

Decisions are rarely cost-free, and it is always worth weighing up the likely advantages and disadvantages of important decisions along the way. Research is rife with trade-offs, because resources such as time, money, expertise and researcher capacity are limited, meaning that once they are spent in one task or process, they are no longer available for others. For example, there is often a trade-off between scope and feasibility, and expanding the scope of a study can potentially compromise the feasibility of conducting it well. Similarly, including additional outcomes can increase the breadth of information collected, but if this comes at the expense of your primary outcome, you have to question whether it is worth it. It is important to consider both the downsides, as well as the benefits of different decisions. This is yet another reason why it is so important to continuously and carefully consider your primary research question, as decisions about the design and conduct of your study should ultimately be judged in terms of how they contribute to your ability to answer it. If it doesn't, then perhaps the trade-off simply isn't worth it for your particular project.

## Take-Home Points {#ch02-take-home-points}

There is a lot to think about when developing your research question and designing a study to address it. The considerations described herein, including progressing from research topic to problem, question, aims and objectives; as well as using frameworks to help design and further refine your research study are intended as a start point from which you can progress. Conducting a research project is more like a marathon (or an ultra-marathon in some cases) than a sprint. You will not have all the answers at the beginning of your journey, nor are you required to. The most important thing is to continue to identify the most pressing problem to be solved at each stage, and to tackle them one by one. To this end, I suggest that you aim to remain both humble and curious throughout the process. Humble, because conducting a research study is difficult and there is always something new to learn, and curious enough to keep learning by reading, attending lectures, and actively participating in research meetings and projects, both within and outside your research group. One of my favorite quotes is by a writer called Maya Angelou, who famously stated "*Do the best you can with what you know, then when you know better, do better*". I believe this is particularly apt throughout the research process -- keep learning and practicing, then apply the knowledge and experience gained to develop and investigate ever more in-depth and robust research questions.
